wtc1f01.author: KELLER
wtc1f01.character: Quiet, unpretentious, intellectually austere; demands spiritual concentration.
wtc1f01.quote: the steps of a second are linked, the fourth and fifth set apart distinctly, larger intervals clearly separated.
wtc1f01.restQuote: The articulation of this subject — and consequently of the fugue-can serve as an example for many of the others
wtc1f01.restSummary: Same rule (seconds linked, fourths/fifths and leaps separated) throughout; in stretti emphasise the leading voice, let the second recede.

wtc1f01.author: BODKY
wtc1f01.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f01.character: Elegant 'showpiece' of continuous stretti, no episodes; for clavichord.
wtc1f01.quote: Legato; the intervals of the fourth and fifth portato

wtc1f01.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f01.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f01.tempoText: provided its tempo be not mistaken (example marked (4 crotchets) per bar; no tempo word or metronome)
wtc1f01.character: Not dry: self-sufficient, contemplative; continuous, not split into sharp members.
wtc1f01.quote: the inner necessity of continuity is thus felt, and consequently a splitting up into too sharply defined members prevented.

wtc1f02.author: KELLER
wtc1f02.tempoText: Quarter note equals 63 (as in the close of the prelude)
wtc1f02.character: Capricious, half-jesting, half-recalcitrant humour; not a Czerny-style pp staccato scherzo.
wtc1f02.quote: in the subject, the mordent-like sixteenths should be linked, the eighth notes set apart with accent, and the syncopation on A flat prepared by two staccato sixteenths.
wtc1f02.restQuote: The notes of the transitional scales are lightly joined, the eighth notes of the two countersubjects lightly separated.
wtc1f02.restSummary: Transitional scales lightly legato; countersubject eighths lightly detached; varied articulation overall.

wtc1f02.author: BODKY
wtc1f02.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f02.character: Regular alternation of developments and episodes; spontaneous inspiration with precise calculation.
wtc1f02.quote: Legato for the "mordent figures"; nonlegato for the eighths; legato for the end of the theme.

wtc1f02.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f02.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f02.character: Sober-minded perseverance, quiet diligence; earnest but graceful.
wtc1f02.quote: The articulation, of itself presenting an alternation between the legato of the melodic intervals and the staccato of the harmonic breaks, increases this impression of perseverance, of quiet diligence
wtc1f02.restSummary: Countersubject never abandons the theme; no articulation given for it.

wtc1f03.author: KELLER
wtc1f03.tempoText: Quarternote equals 84 to 92 (as in the prelude)
wtc1f03.character: Graceful and euphonious, not too fast or brilliant; proud, self-confident close.
wtc1f03.quote: Usually it is played too fast and too brilliantly, losing some of its gracefulness. The subject might be articulated thus:
wtc1f03.restQuote: In bar 7 let the alto part be subordinate to the soprano, in bar 31 the tenor to the bass
wtc1f03.restSummary: Voice balance: subordinate alto in bar 7 and tenor in bar 31; close proud and self-confident.

wtc1f03.author: BODKY
wtc1f03.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f03.quote: The first note staccato; the next five notes slurred; the same for the first four notes of bar 2; all the other notes staccato.

wtc1f03.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f03.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f03.tempoText: Andantino piacevole appears to me to give the right idea of the tempo (rejects Czerny's Allegro crotchet = 104)
wtc1f03.character: Peace and cheerful delight, enchanting, deeply felt; first half expressive, second parlando.
wtc1f03.quote: in the first half it is full of expression and submission, and has a feminine ending, but in the second it changes, so to speak, to a parlando style

wtc1f06.author: KELLER
wtc1f06.character: Strict, violent, aggressive; a controlled allegro marcato.
wtc1f06.quote: The eighth notes of the subject require an accentuated legato; after f in bar 2, a small caesura should be introduced.
wtc1f06.restQuote: on this sixth, b flat', a staccato sign appears-the only autograph one in the first volume
wtc1f06.restSummary: Bach's autograph staccato on the B flat is carried through the whole fugue; trills may begin on the main note.

wtc1f06.author: BODKY
wtc1f06.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f06.character: Constant massing of stretti; theme entrances keep creating surprise; for clavichord.
wtc1f06.quote: Legato; the autographic dash on the b' flat of the second bar should be understood as molto portato.

wtc1f06.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f06.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f06.character: Ingenious; first half advances quietly by steps, second somewhat passionate.
wtc1f06.restQuote: It is one of the finest results of phrase indications that such old established ugly effects disappear, leaving no trace, and are replaced by others of pathetic character.
wtc1f06.restSummary: Proper phrasing of a countersubject passage removes ugly effects.

wtc1f07.author: KELLER
wtc1f07.character: Charming, free and modern; gently moving, not hurried; capricious break after the eighths.
wtc1f07.quote: the eighth notes c"-b flat' in the subject should be separated sharply, the eighth notes e flat"-d" more gently.
wtc1f07.restQuote: The first of the four sixteenth notes should be lightly detached especially in figure (c).
wtc1f07.restSummary: First of each four-sixteenth group lightly detached, especially in the episode figure (c); trills begin on the main note.

wtc1f07.author: BODKY
wtc1f07.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f07.character: Elegant 'secular' fugue; sounds best on the clavichord.

wtc1f07.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f07.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f07.tempoText: must not be taken in hurried tempo
wtc1f07.character: Harmless merry postlude to the prelude; simple and natural.
wtc1f07.restQuote: Anyone who overlooks the connection between the semiquaver following the rest in the upper voice, and the preceding motive, will not give a very smooth rendering
wtc1f07.restSummary: A semiquaver after a rest in an episode belongs to the preceding motive.

wtc1f08.author: KELLER
wtc1f08.character: Spiritually intense, searching; flowing gently, neither dragging nor fluent.
wtc1f08.quote: In the subject itself a light separation of e flat' and a flat' is appropriate to the syncopation of the a flat' without this note's having to be accented.

wtc1f08.author: BODKY
wtc1f08.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f08.character: Inner, not outward grandeur; wealth of feeling; religious background.
wtc1f08.quote: All larger intervals portato, otherwise legato

wtc1f08.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f08.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f08.character: Earnest but milder, softer; noble, deeply pensive, quiet crotchet-quaver movement.
wtc1f08.restSummary: Counterpoint and episodes in quiet quaver steps; no articulation given.

wtc1f12.author: KELLER
wtc1f12.tempoText: Quarter note equals 48 to 56 (as in the prelude)
wtc1f12.character: Deeply earnest, anguished chromatic subject contrasted with calm diatonic episodes.
wtc1f12.quote: the inner cohesion of thought requires a continual legato, as with the theme of the F Minor Fugue in Book I
wtc1f12.restSummary: Bring out the contrast between the chromatic subject entries and the calm diatonic episodes.

wtc1f12.author: BODKY
wtc1f12.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f12.character: Theme symbolizes the cross; 'deathly anguish of the heart'; theme must sing.

wtc1f12.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f12.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f12.character: Deep musing, pensive; measured allabreve movement.
wtc1f12.quote: where a feminine ending would cause the bending of a line, the "ligature" (syncopation) is replaced by a rest, and the end note becomes the starting note of a new motive.
wtc1f12.restQuote: it is impossible to lose sight of the already emphasized Allabreve-character of the theme and to bring out the same in performance, without allowing the small details of a highly expressive figuration to obscure it
wtc1f12.restSummary: Keep the allabreve pulse; the countersubject figuration must not obscure it.

wtc1f13.author: KELLER
wtc1f13.character: Euphonious, soft and gently flowing, not lively.
wtc1f13.quote: One should begin the trill in the subject with the main note in order to avoid the repetition of a note. A suggestion for the articulation of the subject:
wtc1f13.restSummary: The episode example shows the sixteenths in short slurred pairs.

wtc1f13.author: BODKY
wtc1f13.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f13.character: Serene, intimate 'Little Brook' fugue; heavenly serenity; water figures.
wtc1f13.quote: Legato; in the "wave figure," two notes slurred
wtc1f13.restQuote: I personally am convinced that in this particular case Keller found the right version, as can be proved by the great quantity of similar "wave figures"
wtc1f13.restSummary: Theme legato; the four-sixteenth 'wave figure' (from bar 7) slurred two by two (Keller's version).

wtc1f13.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f13.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f13.restSummary: Countersubject clings closely to the theme; second countersubject light, rising.

wtc1f15.author: KELLER
wtc1f15.character: Performer's fugue: uninterrupted tempo, strength, fire, humour, sharp articulation.
wtc1f15.quote: Czerny slurred the quarter notes in the subject c" to b', e" to d", thereby increasing the humor of the fugue; but it is false to Bach's style.
wtc1f15.restQuote: The performance of this fugue requires an uninterrupted tempo strength and fire, also something of humor (especially with the inversion of the leap of the seventh of the subject) and sharp articulation.
wtc1f15.restSummary: Sharp articulation throughout; humour, especially in the inverted leap of the seventh.

wtc1f15.author: BODKY
wtc1f15.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f15.quote: See Example A4. All runs of sixteenths leggiero

wtc1f15.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f15.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f15.tempoText: Con moto giojoso (quaver beat); tempo 'somewhat rapid'
wtc1f15.character: Truly jesting game; untroubled joy, brisk as bees.

wtc1f17.author: KELLER
wtc1f17.character: Noble and warm, organ- or choral-like; solemnly slow, not dragging.
wtc1f17.quote: An upbeat reading (with a caesura after the third eighth note) would destroy its peace, for the entire fugue requires a continuous legato and provides only a few pauses for breath.
wtc1f17.restQuote: the entire fugue requires a continuous legato and provides only a few pauses for breath.

wtc1f17.author: BODKY
wtc1f17.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f17.quote: The eighths legato e portato, the rest legato

wtc1f17.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f17.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f17.character: Thoughtful, tender; joyful repose; the sensitive dreamer.
wtc1f17.restQuote: wonderfully does Bach make varied use of the motives here marked off by slurs
wtc1f17.restSummary: Riemann's slurs mark off motives; counterpoint in smooth semiquaver scale movement.

wtc1f18.author: KELLER
wtc1f18.character: Expressive but graceful; free, almost romantic subject.
wtc1f18.quote: The subject is legato except for the repeated eighth notes, which are lightly separated.

wtc1f18.author: BODKY
wtc1f18.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f18.quote: The first seven notes legato, the two next ones slurred, the rest of the theme slight portato.

wtc1f18.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f18.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f18.character: One of the most expressive; subjective feeling, natural, a noble humour.
wtc1f18.quote: at the end, conforms to the staccato-character of the theme.
wtc1f18.restQuote: Its smooth crotchets introduce more repose into the piece, and the syncopation at the end gives opportunity for syncopation on an extended scale in several of the episodes.
wtc1f18.restSummary: Second countersubject in smooth crotchets; first countersubject ends staccato like the theme.

wtc1f21.author: KELLER
wtc1f21.character: Capricious, humorous strict dance with lively rhythm; scherzando.
wtc1f21.quote: How should one articulate the subject? According to Czerny (that is the most common and perhaps the conception most suitable to the scherzando character of the fugue).
wtc1f21.restQuote: The notes of the first countersubject should be individually articulated.
wtc1f21.restSummary: First countersubject articulated note by note; in bars 15-18 and 39-40 the second-countersubject eighths may take a light finger staccato.

wtc1f21.author: BODKY
wtc1f21.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f21.character: Complicated fugue with two plastic countersubjects; brilliant writing for the harpsichord.
wtc1f21.quote: Nonlegato for the eighths, except for the two falling seconds d-c and e flat-d, which should be slurred; the sixteenths leggiero.

wtc1f21.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f21.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f21.character: Pleasing, unpretending, harmonious; a true garland of flowers.
wtc1f21.restQuote: hardnesses requiring special phrasing to make them sound euphonious do not occur.
wtc1f21.restSummary: Easy, euphonious; episodes spin out the climbing figuration of the theme.

wtc1f24.author: KELLER
wtc1f24.character: Solemn, broad largo; severe, laden with Affekt; the 'sigh-motive' subject.
wtc1f24.quote: The significance of the little slurs in the subject, which are original, is obvious; the note of resolution should be played somewhat shorter and weaker.

wtc1f24.author: BODKY
wtc1f24.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f24.character: Mourning; cross symbol in the theme; descending seconds express weeping.
wtc1f24.quote: The first three notes legato e portato, the rest slurred in pairs (autographic).

wtc1f24.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f24.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f24.character: Faust-like search after truth, a soul-struggle; earnest, not mere misery.
wtc1f24.quote: the major thirds which, in place of the expected minor harmonies appearing as resolutions of appoggiaturas ... should be somewhat emphasized, as they are not plain end notes, but rather substitutes for end notes

wtc1f04.author: BODKY
wtc1f04.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f04.character: Monumental, organ-like; 'seriously and with increasing animation'; theme a cross and B-A-C-H allusion.
wtc1f04.quote: Molto legato for first theme and entire first part, legato for the other themes.
wtc1f04.restSummary: Second and third themes legato (first theme and whole first part molto legato).

wtc1f04.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f04.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f04.tempoText: Sostenuto ma non troppo, in minim (half-note) beats; Czerny's crotchet = 112 'utterly mistaken'
wtc1f04.character: Majestic cathedral, colossal dignity; semibreve theme under powerful restraint.

wtc1f05.author: BODKY
wtc1f05.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f05.character: Pompous, French-overture style; suited to the full harpsichord.
wtc1f05.restQuote: we feel very hesitant to recommend the exaggerated "French dotting" suggested by Dolmetsch and used by the majority of harpsichordists.
wtc1f05.restSummary: Marcato e quasi legato; no exaggerated French over-dotting.

wtc1f05.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f05.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f05.character: Powerful, proud, resolute; energetic demisemiquaver run and persistent dotting.

wtc1f09.author: BODKY
wtc1f09.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f09.character: Vocal in idiom, not far from the 'Gratias agimus' of the B minor Mass.
wtc1f09.quote: The first eighth of the theme always staccato, the next note tenuto, the sixteenths leggiero.
wtc1f09.restQuote: The "sighs" in the tenor, bars 13-16, and in the soprano, bars 22-25, should be emphasized.
wtc1f09.restSummary: Sigh figures in tenor bars 13-16 and soprano 22-25 emphasized.

wtc1f09.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f09.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f09.character: Joy of a wandering life; resolution, active energy.

wtc1f10.author: BODKY
wtc1f10.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f10.character: Brilliant two-part fugue; a lively display of tone colours.

wtc1f10.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f10.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f10.character: Somewhat mournful yet contemplative, like nature in autumn.
wtc1f10.quote: The actual motive (see the notes marked with upward stems), clearly perceptible through the continued semiquaver movement, actually makes the fugue more or less in 3, instead of 2 voices (which must of course be attended to in performance).

wtc1f11.author: BODKY
wtc1f11.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f11.character: Passepied-like dance; a much less serious affair than the C major fugue.
wtc1f11.quote: The upbeat always portato, the first two eighths of the first bar slurred, the third eighth staccato; all the other notes legato.
wtc1f11.restQuote: Keller advises playing the upbeats in the themes of the F major Fugue, W.K. I, and the B minor Fugue, W.K. II, legato
wtc1f11.restSummary: Bodky rejects Keller's slurred upbeat: a one-note upbeat is never slurred to the next note.

wtc1f11.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f11.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f11.tempoText: Andantino piacevole (beat: quaver up-beat to crotchet)
wtc1f11.character: Simple, unpretentious, pleasant; theme like a fish resting on a smooth wave.

wtc1f14.author: BODKY
wtc1f14.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f14.character: Pensive, lovelorn sadness; countersubject symbolizes teardrops.
wtc1f14.restQuote: in the countersubject first note light portato, the falling or rising seconds slurred in pairs, the rest legato.
wtc1f14.restSummary: Countersubject: first note light portato, the seconds slurred in pairs, otherwise legato.

wtc1f14.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f14.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f14.tempoText: Lento e mesto (minim beat); 'such super-abundance of harmony requires slow tempo'
wtc1f14.character: Pain and torture, struggling upward through chromatic harmonies.

wtc1f16.author: BODKY
wtc1f16.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f16.character: Molto energico, not molto tranquillo; faster than printed editions advise.
wtc1f16.quote: First two eighths legato, the two quarters tenuto, the sixteenths leggiero (the eighth between them, of course, nonlegato).
wtc1f16.restQuote: Bach himself shows, in the last bar, that he reckons with nonlegato playing
wtc1f16.restSummary: Bodky reads nonlegato playing from Bach's last bar; the whole piece is energetic.

wtc1f16.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f16.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f16.character: Pensive earnestness; feminine ending and accented rest are essential.
wtc1f16.quote: the absence of the feminine ending in the first half, and of the (accented) rest at the beginning of the second, are heavy losses.
wtc1f16.restQuote: If we articulate Bach's countersubject more precisely, we find first a syncopated motive (the g before the rest produces an effect quite similar to a note held over, only more striking, more sobbing)
wtc1f16.restSummary: Countersubject: syncopated, 'sobbing' opening motive; ascending motive clarifies the accented rest.

wtc1f19.author: BODKY
wtc1f19.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f19.quote: The first note tenuto, molto legato for the eighths ... Keller's suggestion that a comma be inserted after the eleventh note of the soprano part.
wtc1f19.restQuote: legato for the sixteenths which may frequently be subdivided into three legato and three leggiero notes.
wtc1f19.restSummary: Sixteenths legato, often split into three legato plus three leggiero.

wtc1f19.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f19.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f19.tempoText: Poco lento, con molto espressivo; coda 'should be taken in quiet tempo'
wtc1f19.character: Heartfelt feeling, touching naivete; very quiet and expressive rendering.
wtc1f19.quote: if only the rhythmical nature of the theme and the feminine endings of its several motives be properly recognized and understood

wtc1f20.author: BODKY
wtc1f20.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f20.character: Among Bach's 'wild' A minor pieces, where the virtuoso element prevails.
wtc1f20.quote: See Example A5. In general nonlegato; più legato only for the beautiful episode, bars 40-42.
wtc1f20.restQuote: più legato only for the beautiful episode, bars 40-42.
wtc1f20.restSummary: Generally nonlegato; more legato only in the episode bars 40-42.

wtc1f20.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f20.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f20.character: Somewhat colourless, light see-saw; little rhythmic energy.

wtc1f22.author: BODKY
wtc1f22.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f22.quote: First two notes molto tenuto, the others ben legato

wtc1f22.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f22.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f22.character: Same holy earnestness; solemn descent, very free metre.
wtc1f22.quote: this is especially true in the fugue under notice, of the first minim of the theme, which, without doubt, bears the stronger accent

wtc1f23.author: BODKY
wtc1f23.work: The Interpretation of Bach's Keyboard Works
wtc1f23.quote: Legato with slight tenuto for the last two eighths of the theme

wtc1f23.author: RIEMANN
wtc1f23.work: Analysis of J. S. Bach's Wohltemperirtes Clavier (1890; Eng. 1893)
wtc1f23.character: Simple, easily understood, somewhat conventional; plagal around the tonic.
wtc1f23.restSummary: Countersubject's characteristic feature is a trailing scale passage.
